title: Rights and Provenance in AI Art
answer: Copyright and trademark, licensing, training data and opt-outs, studio security, and content credentials.

children.name: Copyright and Trademark for AI Work
children.blurb: This page covers how copyright and trademark law applies to work made with or by AI systems, from text-to-image outputs to music and video.

children.name: Licensing Synthetic Media
children.blurb: Licensing synthetic media covers the rights to use, modify, distribute, and monetize outputs made by generative systems, plus the inputs and model weights that produce them.

children.name: Training Data and Opt-Outs
children.blurb: Training data and opt-outs covers the sources used to teach generative image, video, and audio models, and the ways creators can ask that their work be excluded.

children.name: Security for Creative Studios
children.blurb: Security for creative studios covers the protection of creative assets, including AI models, training data, generated works, and the studio's own intellectual property.

children.name: Watermarking and Content Credentials
children.blurb: Watermarking and content credentials cover methods that attach provenance and origin information to AI generated or edited media.

sections.body: This section covers the legal and practical machinery that decides who owns, who may use, and who can prove the origin of AI generated images, video, audio and text. In practice the work here is less about philosophy and more about paperwork, model settings, and metadata. Studios check whether a generator was trained on licensed material, artists look for opt-out registries, and platforms attach provenance signals to files at export. Rights questions now arrive at the start of a project rather than after a dispute, because the training data behind a model shapes what a client will accept. The field sits where intellectual property law, model supply chains and creative production meet.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Copyright offices and courts have settled some narrow points, mainly that purely machine generated output with no human authorship has no copyright, while human selection and arrangement can qualify. Trademark is more settled in practice, since brand owners can act against confusing output even when copyright is unclear. What remains open is the status of training on scraped works, the scope of fair use or its equivalents, and how liability is split between model makers and users. Opt-outs exist but are uneven, and there is no single registry that covers every model. Watermarking and content credentials are useful signals, not proof, since they can be stripped or forged. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, which shows how much of the field is still being argued rather than decided.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Start with Copyright and Trademark for AI Work for the baseline rules on authorship, infringement and brand confusion. Licensing Synthetic Media then translates those rules into contract terms for clients, stock libraries and platforms. Training Data and Opt-Outs goes upstream to the datasets and the mechanisms artists use to exclude their work. Security for Creative Studios covers the operational side, including leaks, model theft and access control inside production teams. Watermarking and Content Credentials closes the loop by explaining how provenance is recorded and checked after a file leaves the studio. Read together, they trace a work from training corpus to signed export.
